content: Acetylcholinesterase, also referred to as AChE, is an enzyme in humans that is encoded by the acetylcholinesterase gene. This enzyme plays a critical role in the nervous system by hydrolyzing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions and cholinergic synapses in the brain. By breaking down acetylcholine, acetylcholinesterase effectively terminates signal transmission between nerve cells and muscles or within the brain. In addition to its role in the nervous system, acetylcholinesterase is also present on the membranes of red blood cells, where it serves as the Yt blood group antigen. The enzyme exists in several molecular forms, all of which share similar catalytic properties but differ in their structural organization and how they attach to cell surfaces. These variations arise from alternative splicing of the AChE gene's mRNA and post-translational modifications that involve the assembly of catalytic and structural subunits. The predominant form of acetylcholinesterase found in the brain, muscles, and other tissues is a hydrophilic variant. This form forms disulfide-linked oligomers that associate with structural subunits containing either collagenous or lipid components. Another form of acetylcholinesterase, which is alternatively spliced and primarily expressed in erythroid (red blood cell-producing) tissues, differs at its C-terminal end. This variant includes a cleavable hydrophobic peptide with a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor site, allowing it to attach to cell membranes via phosphoinositide (PI) moieties that are added after translation. Acetylcholinesterase is also a critical target for nerve agents, such as organophosphates. These agents inhibit the enzyme's function, preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine. This leads to continuous stimulation of muscles, resulting in prolonged and uncontrollable muscle contractions throughout the body, which can be life-threatening.
